column2: An opening snap after S2, with a loud S1 and apical mid-diastolic rumble, is mitral stenosis; the shorter the S2–snap interval, the more severe the stenosis.
Significant chronic AR gives a wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic), so 120/95 mmHg argues against it. Acute AR may have a near-normal pulse pressure.
Exertional dyspnoea and PND with an apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla is mitral regurgitation (rheumatic or prolapse in the young); echo confirms.
Early diastolic murmur with wide pulse pressure is AR; the apical rumble is an Austin Flint murmur, told from MS by a normal S1 and no opening snap.
Echo (TTE/TOE) and catheterisation define a chronic valve lesion; cardiac enzymes detect myocardial necrosis and say nothing about valve disease.
Loud P2, RV heave and RVH with functional TR (normal leaflets) means pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure; then find its cause.
A displaced apex with a soft S1 in rheumatic disease is mitral regurgitation (LV volume overload). MS gives a loud S1 and tapping undisplaced apex.
Long-standing MS causes pulmonary hypertension and RV failure (raised JVP, RV heave, hepatomegaly, oedema); this indicates valvotomy or surgery.
In MS the apex is undisplaced and tapping (a palpable loud S1) because the LV is protected from overload.
Pulmonary hypertension causes a loud (even palpable) P2, often with an RV heave. The opening snap and loud S1 come from the mitral valve itself.
Balloon mitral commissurotomy: symptomatic MS (area ≤ 1.5 cm²) with pliable non-calcified leaflets, ≤ mild MR and no LA thrombus on TOE.
In MS with sinus rhythm, atrial contraction causes pre-systolic accentuation of the rumble; it disappears when AF develops.
A basal systolic thrill with an ejection murmur in an elderly man is most likely calcific aortic stenosis; echo grades severity.
Pulse pressure 120 mmHg with significant AR gives hyperdynamic signs: collapsing pulse, Corrigan, de Musset (head nodding), Quincke and Duroziez.
Symptomatic severe AS has ~50% 2-year mortality without replacement; at prohibitive surgical risk, refer for TAVI (heart-team assessment).
Ejection systolic murmur at the upper right sternal edge radiating to the carotids is aortic stenosis; angina, dyspnoea and syncope signal severe disease.
Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge louder on inspiration, with a raised JVP and large v waves, is tricuspid regurgitation.
Transthoracic echo with Doppler confirms AS and grades it (velocity, gradient, area) with LV function; angiography is done before surgery.
In MS the enlarged LA straightens the left heart border, gives a double right border and splays (widens) the carina; upper-lobe diversion and Kerley B lines.
Ectopia lentis, pectus, high palate and hypermobility suggest Marfan syndrome, commonly with MVP; aortic root dilatation is the dangerous lesion.
Mitral murmurs are loudest at the apex with the patient in the left lateral position; MR is pansystolic, radiates to the axilla, louder in expiration.
Mid-systolic click then late systolic murmur is mitral valve prolapse (Barlow); standing/Valsalva bring the click earlier, squatting delays it.
MS signs: malar flush, AF, tapping apex, loud S1, opening snap, RV heave. A pansystolic murmur to the axilla is mitral regurgitation.
MVP is systolic displacement of a leaflet > 2 mm into the LA; most are asymptomatic and need no drugs, but echo follow-up is advised.
Bioprosthetic valves degenerate after ~10 years (earlier in mitral position); a new apical diastolic murmur means prosthetic MS. Exclude endocarditis; redo or valve-in-valve.
Dyspnoea, AF and haemoptysis with an apical diastolic rumble is mitral stenosis, usually a late consequence of childhood rheumatic fever.
Severe MR with pulmonary oedema and adequate BP: IV afterload reduction (nitroprusside/nitrates) increases forward flow; IABP if hypotensive; then surgery.
Dental prophylaxis (AHA/ESC) only for highest risk: prosthetic valves, previous IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD. NICE does not recommend it routinely.
Mechanical valves need lifelong warfarin (INR ~2.5–3.5 mitral, 2.0–3.0 bileaflet aortic). DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN).
A pansystolic murmur louder on inspiration (Carvallo) is tricuspid regurgitation; in Marfan it may follow tricuspid prolapse.
TR (e.g. right-sided IE in drug users) gives giant v (cv) waves in the JVP and a pulsatile liver. Cannon a waves mean AV dissociation.
A bisferiens (double-peaked) pulse occurs in mixed aortic valve disease with predominant AR, severe AR and HOCM. Pure AS gives a slow-rising pulse.
Severe calcific AS gives a soft or absent A2 (and reversed splitting). Pulmonary hypertension gives a loud P2; ASD gives fixed splitting.
AR arises from leaflet disease (rheumatic, IE, bicuspid) or root dilatation (Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, syphilis). DCM causes functional MR/TR.
Pulmonary stenosis: ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge, louder on inspiration, with click and soft P2; balloon valvuloplasty if severe.
Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds and pulsus paradoxus with RA collapse is tamponade (likely malignant): urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis. Diuretics are harmful.
Positional pain, friction rub and concave ST elevation across several territories is acute pericarditis; treat with aspirin/NSAID plus colchicine.
A new raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus and hypotension days after pericarditis means tamponade; confirm with echo and drain urgently.
Echo shows the effusion, RA/RV diastolic collapse and a plethoric IVC, and guides pericardiocentesis. ECG and CXR are insensitive.
Tamponade with hypotension needs urgent pericardiocentesis; diuretics, nitrates and ACEi worsen filling. Fluids only as a bridge.
In rheumatic fever, carditis and recurrence are commonest when the first attack is in young children, so young age is a bad sign; penicillin prophylaxis prevents recurrence.
Duke major criteria: persistently positive blood cultures (e.g. 3 sets ≥ 1 h apart) or imaging evidence of endocardial involvement. IVDU and emboli are minor.
